clinicalPearls: Emerges when bulky, rapidly proliferating tumours (especially high-grade lymphomas and acute leukemias) undergo massive cell death, either spontaneously or within hours to days of starting cytotoxic therapy
Classic biochemical tetrad is hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hypocalcemia
Risk correlates with tumour bulk, proliferation rate, and baseline chemosensitivity - Burkitt lymphoma and acute lymphoblastic leukemia carry the highest risk
Pre-existing renal impairment, volume depletion, and acidic urine markedly increase risk of uric acid nephropathy
Onset is typically 12-72 hours after initiating effective therapy but can occur before any treatment is given in highly proliferative tumours
Acute kidney injury is usually the dominant clinical threat, driven by uric acid and/or calcium phosphate precipitation in renal tubules
Cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia is the most immediately life-threatening complication
Aggressive risk stratification and prophylaxis before chemotherapy is far more effective than treating established syndrome
harrison.pathophysiology: Rapid destruction of malignant cells releases large quantities of intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the circulation. Nucleic acid catabolism generates a surge of uric acid that can precipitate in the relatively acidic, low-flow environment of the renal tubules, producing obstructive nephropathy. Hyperphosphatemia from cell lysis exceeds the solubility product for calcium phosphate, causing tissue and renal deposition and consequent hypocalcemia. The resulting acute kidney injury further impairs excretion of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, creating a self-amplifying metabolic crisis.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis-associated multiorgan dysfunction with acute kidney injury
Chemotherapy-induced acute kidney injury from nephrotoxic agents
Acute uric acid nephropathy unrelated to malignancy
infectionMimics: Severe sepsis with acute kidney injury and metabolic derangement mimicking the electrolyte pattern of TLS
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute kidney injury from contrast nephropathy or nephrotoxic drugs
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid - core panel to confirm the metabolic tetrad and grade severity
Creatinine and estimated GFR - assess renal function and monitor for acute kidney injury
ECG - screen for hyperkalemia- or hypocalcemia-related conduction changes and arrhythmia risk
Urinalysis and urine output monitoring - detect early oliguria or uric acid crystalluria
LDH - surrogate marker of tumour burden and cell turnover, useful for risk stratification
Baseline and serial renal function before and during cytoreductive therapy
Coagulation profile if disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected concurrently
redFlags: Oliguria or rising creatinine suggesting evolving acute kidney injury
ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS, QT prolongation) indicating hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia
Rapidly rising potassium or phosphate despite supportive measures
High tumour bulk with elevated baseline LDH and uric acid before therapy initiation
Need for urgent renal replacement therapy in refractory metabolic derangement
pitfalls: Assuming TLS only occurs after chemotherapy - spontaneous lysis can precede any treatment in highly proliferative tumours
Correcting hypocalcemia aggressively without addressing hyperphosphatemia first, which can worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation
Underestimating risk in patients with bulky, chemosensitive tumours and pre-existing renal impairment or dehydration
Delaying prophylactic measures until after laboratory abnormalities appear rather than initiating them proactively
harrison.prognosis: With prompt recognition, risk stratification, and preventive management, most cases resolve without permanent renal impairment; outcomes worsen substantially once oliguric acute kidney injury or refractory hyperkalemia develops, occasionally requiring dialysis.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Oncologic Emergencies (Tumor Lysis Syndrome)
